messages.subject: Issue indexing in NIMBLE
parts:
Hi all,

I'm trying to index an array in my nimble code by accessing the value of a different array at the value I am looping through. Code fragment is below:

for (n in 1:S_n) {
    logit(p[S[n]]) <- alpha_0 + delta_a[S[n]] + inprod(alpha[1:C_a], X_a[n,1:C_a])
}

When I "assemble" the model using the nimbleModel() function, I get the following error:
Defining model
Error : Error processing model: something is wrong with the index S[n].
Indexing in model code requires this syntax: '(start expression):(end expression)'.
Error: Error occurred defining  p[S[n]]

I tried to fix this issue by assigning S[n] to a new value and using that as the index:

for (n in 1:S_n) {
    s <- S[n]
    logit(p[s]) <- alpha_0 + delta_a[s] + inprod(alpha[1:C_a], X_a[n,1:C_a])
}

But, this also results in errors:
Defining model
Error in p[s[iAns]] <- origIDs[iAns] : object 's' not found
In addition: Warning messages:
1: In min(x, na.rm = na.rm) :
  no non-missing arguments to min; returning Inf
2: In max(x, na.rm = na.rm) :
  no non-missing arguments to max; returning -Inf
3: In min(x, na.rm = na.rm) :
  no non-missing arguments to min; returning Inf
4: In max(x, na.rm = na.rm) :
  no non-missing arguments to max; returning -Inf
5: In genExpandedNodeAndParentNames3(debug = debug) :
  Multiple definitions for the same node. Did you forget indexing with 'n' on the left-hand side of 's <- S[n]'?
6: In genExpandedNodeAndParentNames3(debug = debug) :
  Multiple definitions for the same node. Did you forget indexing with 'n' on the left-hand side of 'p[s] <- expit(alpha_0 + delta_a[s] + inprod(alpha[1:1], X_a[n, 1:1]))'?

I don't think that reproducible code is necessary to answer the question, but if someone wants it I can provide it. I think it just requires someone who is more familiar with indexing in NIMBLE.

Thanks in advance!

messages.author: 39971e2c19b8ec70
messages.subject: Re: Issue indexing in NIMBLE
parts:
Dear Andrew,

I am certainly not the best person to answer this, but I struggled with indexing in Nimble myself, and what solved it, was to declare everything related to that as `constants' instead of as `data'. I.e., do you provide the `S' variable to the nimbleModel() function in `data' or in `constants`? For me to put it in `constants` solved the problems. 

Let me know if that helped, if not, you will have to wait for more educated answer.

Regards,

Tomas

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: Issue indexing in NIMBLE
parts:
I think that's a good suggestion.

When model code has nested indexing on the right-hand side (RHS) vs left-hand side (LHS), the situations are quite different.

On the RHS, say

y[i] <- delta[S[i]]

then S[i] might be constants, data, or a latent state.  And in any of those cases it may have duplicate entries.  If it is constants, the model relationships (which element of delta each y[i] depends on) are fixed; all steps will be faster in this case.  If it is latent state (there is a stochastic declaration with S[i] on the LHS elsewhere in the model), then we call it dynamic or stochastic indexing, and the S[i]s are sampled by MCMC (and everything will run slower, because really each y[i] depends potentially on any element of delta, so avoid this if it's not necessary).  If it is data, the S[i] won't be sampled but the computations will still be slower.  I think we warning-trap this case and suggest making the nested index (S[i]) a constant instead of data.

On the LHS, say

y[S[i]] <- delta[i]

S[i] must be constants and must have no duplicate entries.  It must be constants because we don't support stochastic dependencies that would arise if it isn't; they don't make as much sense.  There must be no duplicate entries because there can't be two declarations for the same element of y.

So another problem could be if you have S as constants but have duplicate entries.

More about the distinction between data and constants can be found in our user manual.

I hope the bit of explanation helps clarify things.

Perry

I had neglected to include S in either the constants or the data, so I added it to the list of constants. But, there is now an issue with multiple definitions for some nodes, and I don't understand the reason that is happening. Here is the full code, as I think it is more important now:

occ_code = nimbleCode({
 
  # First time period - no autoregression
for (n in 1:S_n) {

# Occupancy probability
    logit(psi[n]) <- beta_0 + inprod(beta[1:C_b], X_b[n,1:C_b]) + delta_b[S[n]]
   
    # Presence
    Z[n] ~ dbern(psi[n])
   
    # Detection probability
logit(p[S[n]]) <- alpha_0 + delta_a[S[n]] + inprod(alpha[1:C_a], X_a[n,1:C_a])

# Recorded
    Y[n] ~ dbern(Z[n] * p[S[n]])
  }
 
  # With autoregression (gamma * psi[n-S_n])
  for (n in (S_n+1):N) {
   
    # Occupancy probability
    logit(psi[n]) <- beta_0 + inprod(beta[1:C_b], X_b[n,1:C_b]) + delta_b[S[n]] +
      (gamma * psi[n-S_n])
   
    # Presence
    Z[n] ~ dbern(psi[n])
   
    # Detection probability
logit(p[S[n]]) <- alpha_0 + delta_a[S[n]] + inprod(alpha[1:C_a], X_a[n,1:C_a])

# Recorded
    Y[n] ~ dbern(Z[n] * p[S[n]])
  }
 
  # Priors
  for (c in 1:C_b) {
    beta[c] ~ dnorm(0, tau = 0.01)
  }
  beta_0 ~ dnorm(0, tau = 0.01)
 
  for (c in 1:C_a) {
    alpha[c] ~ dnorm(0, tau = 0.01)
  }
  alpha_0 ~ dnorm(0, tau = 0.01)
 
  for (s in 1:S_n) {
    delta_b[s] ~ dnorm(0, tau = 0.01)
    delta_a[s] ~ dnorm(0, tau = 0.01)
  }
 
  gamma ~ T(dnorm(0, 0.01), 0, 1)
})

occ_constants = list(N=N, C_b=C_b, C_a=C_a, S_n=S_n, S=S)

occ_model = nimbleModel(occ_code, constants = occ_constants, dimensions = list(X_b = c(N, C_b),
                                                                               X_a = c(N, C_a),
                                                                               Y = N))

messages.subject: Re: Issue indexing in NIMBLE
parts: It looks like in
for (n in 1:S_n)

you have declarations for p[1]...p[242]
and then in
for (n in (S_n+1):N)

you again have declarations for p[1]...p[242]

That would be duplicate declarations.  I'm not sure if there is a confusion about how the model language works or just a coding confusion.  The model language is a declarative language.  That means it doesn't matter in what order declarations appear.  The declarations are putting together a graphical model.  It is not allowed to declare the same node twice.  I am wondering if you want p[n] instead of p[S[n]].

Perry

On Friday, October 7, 2022 at 9:39:23 AM UTC-6 pdevalpine wrote:
I think that's a good suggestion.

When model code has nested indexing on the right-hand side (RHS) vs left-hand side (LHS), the situations are quite different.

On the RHS, say

y[i] <- delta[S[i]]

then S[i] might be constants, data, or a latent state.  And in any of those cases it may have duplicate entries.  If it is constants, the model relationships (which element of delta each y[i] depends on) are fixed; all steps will be faster in this case.  If it is latent state (there is a stochastic declaration with S[i] on the LHS elsewhere in the model), then we call it dynamic or stochastic indexing, and the S[i]s are sampled by MCMC (and everything will run slower, because really each y[i] depends potentially on any element of delta, so avoid this if it's not necessary).  If it is data, the S[i] won't be sampled but the computations will still be slower.  I think we warning-trap this case and suggest making the nested index (S[i]) a constant instead of data.

On the LHS, say

y[S[i]] <- delta[i]

S[i] must be constants and must have no duplicate entries.  It must be constants because we don't support stochastic dependencies that would arise if it isn't; they don't make as much sense.  There must be no duplicate entries because there can't be two declarations for the same element of y.

So another problem could be if you have S as constants but have duplicate entries.

More about the distinction between data and constants can be found in our user manual.

I hope the bit of explanation helps clarify things.

Perry

It looks like in

and then in 
for (n in (S_n+1):N)
you again have declarations for p[1]...p[242]

That would be duplicate declarations.  I'm not sure if there is a confusion about how the model language works or just a coding confusion.  The model language is a declarative language.  That means it doesn't matter in what order declarations appear.  The declarations are putting together a graphical model.  It is not allowed to declare the same node twice.  I am wondering if you want p[n] instead of p[S[n]].

Perry
